category.label: Citrulline
category.comparisonNote: Free L-citrulline and citrulline malate are distinct label profiles. Malate compound mass and a declared ratio are not converted to free L-citrulline. Compare the same form and verified label serving; a nitric-oxide mechanism or ingredient cost does not establish exercise benefit.

guide.title: Citrulline: separate L-citrulline from citrulline malate
guide.summary: The label can describe free L-citrulline or a citrulline-malate material. Their full weights are not interchangeable active amounts.
guide.evidence: A 2026 synthesis found a small average exercise effect for citrulline malate, with low to very low certainty. A trial matching delivered citrulline did not demonstrate a clear added malate advantage in its tested outcomes. A nitric-oxide pathway does not guarantee a useful workout effect.
guide.limitations: Studies differ in composition, exercise tests and participants, and many findings are not robust. A ratio on the front of a pack does not verify its actual composition. Evidence for one form or protocol cannot automatically be transferred to another.
guide.catalogReading: Keep full citrulline-malate compound mass separate from explicitly declared L-citrulline. This catalog does not convert a nominal 2:1 or other ratio into inferred free L-citrulline or rank equal grams of both forms as equivalent. Check label serving and overlap with pre-workout and arginine.
guide.safety: Gastrointestinal discomfort can occur, and long-term safety data are limited. Review medicines and medical conditions with a clinician before using it, particularly where blood-pressure treatment is involved. Do not use a pump claim to replace medical assessment.
guide.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: After absorption, citrulline can be converted to arginine, particularly by the kidneys.
Arginine can supply nitric-oxide production, which participates in normal regulation of blood vessels. Malate has a separate metabolic role.
A plausible pathway and higher circulating amino-acid levels do not establish improved strength, recovery or a benefit from the added malate.
guide.treatment: These sports studies do not establish citrulline as a treatment for cardiovascular disease, erectile dysfunction or persistent fatigue. Medical use requires condition-specific evidence and supervision.
guide.whoMayBenefit: An adult evaluating a specific performance outcome can review the modest, uncertain findings with a qualified sports professional. The evidence does not identify a group that must take it routinely or prove a deficiency from poor performance.
guide.routineUse: No universal need for a citrulline supplement is established. Treat a pre-workout blend, isolated citrulline and arginine as possible overlapping exposures to review, rather than automatic additions to one stack.

whoCanConsider: Healthy adult athletes with a defined exercise test or training objective can consider the small, uncertain performance findings.
Adults comparing isolated L-citrulline with citrulline malate or a pre-workout can examine declared ingredient amounts and form without assuming equal grams are equivalent.
whoShouldReview: People using blood-pressure or other relevant medicines, or with cardiovascular or kidney conditions, need individual review.
People with unexplained fatigue or symptoms attributed to poor circulation need assessment rather than a pump supplement.
Under-18s, pregnancy and breastfeeding require guidance beyond an adult sports-product comparison.
buyingGuide.foodSummary: Watermelon supplies citrulline. Its content varies, and a normal fruit portion or juice serving is not assumed to match an isolated L-citrulline or citrulline-malate amount.

foods.name: Watermelon juice used in a controlled feeding study
foods.detail: Study-specific juice composition, not a universal value for watermelon flesh, rind or a commercial juice. This portion is not an intake recommendation.
foods.quantityNote: Retains the source serving and preparation; not a supplement-dose equivalent.

value.targetedUse: An otherwise healthy adult evaluating an optional, measurable exercise-performance benefit after training and nutrition are adequate.
value.reason: The latest citrulline-malate synthesis found a small average effect with low to very low certainty. That supports at most a situational purchase, without a reliable benefit or proof that malate is superior.
worthWhen: The buyer has a specific outcome and accepts that a benefit may be small or absent.
The label distinguishes free L-citrulline from full citrulline-malate mass, and overlap with pre-workout or arginine is reviewed.
skipWhen: The purchase relies on a pump claim, an assumed conversion of a nominal ratio, or treating compound grams as free L-citrulline.
It crowds out higher-priority food, training or recovery needs.
value.scope: Applies to an optional adult exercise goal. Evidence and amounts for L-citrulline and citrulline malate remain separate; the score does not rate treatment of a medical condition.

dos.title: Identify free or compound content
dos.detail: Keep explicitly declared L-citrulline separate from full citrulline-malate mass when comparing products.

dos.title: Review the outcome and overlap
dos.detail: Choose a specific exercise outcome to assess and check any citrulline or arginine already in a pre-workout.

donts.title: Don't infer content from a nominal ratio
donts.detail: A citrulline-malate ratio alone does not verify free L-citrulline or make equal compound weights equivalent.

donts.title: Don't treat a pump as a clinical result
donts.detail: A sensation or blood-flow claim does not establish treatment benefit or justify displacing higher-priority food and recovery needs.

intakeGuide.summary: No established dietary requirement or universal performance dose. Free L-citrulline and citrulline malate amounts cannot be treated as equivalent.
notes: No automatic dose increase is assigned for training frequency or experience.

medicalGuide.summary: Condition-specific evidence, separate from sports benefits and purchase priority.

conditions.findings: Exercise and blood-flow findings do not establish a treatment indication for these conditions.
conditions.limits: These sports studies do not establish citrulline as a treatment for cardiovascular disease, erectile dysfunction or persistent fatigue. Medical use requires condition-specific evidence and supervision.

pathway.title: Citrulline supplies arginine through the kidneys
pathway.summary: Citrulline can raise the supply of arginine, which is used in nitric-oxide signalling. Citrulline malate also contains malate; its total mass is not all L-citrulline.

steps.label: Absorbed citrulline enters the circulation
steps.detail: Oral L-citrulline is absorbed and becomes available for tissue metabolism.

steps.label: Kidneys convert citrulline into arginine
steps.detail: Renal metabolism converts circulating citrulline into arginine and releases arginine into the blood.

steps.label: Arginine supplies nitric-oxide production
steps.detail: Cells can use arginine as a substrate for nitric-oxide synthesis.

steps.label: Nitric oxide participates in vascular signalling
steps.detail: Nitric oxide helps regulate blood-vessel relaxation. A change in this pathway is not itself a performance result.

pathway.caveat: Malate is a separate metabolic component; this diagram does not establish an added malate benefit. Higher blood arginine does not guarantee better strength, recovery or endurance.
